short: The total value of everything in your account right now.
detail: It adds up what your investments are worth today and any cash you have. It changes on days the market is open.
example: If your investments are worth $900 and you have $100 in cash, your balance is $1,000.

short: Money you move from your bank into your investing account.
detail: A deposit lands as cash first. If auto-invest is on, it then buys your chosen mix for you.
example: You move $150 from your bank on the first of each month.

short: A deposit that happens on its own on the same day each month.
detail: You set it up once. After that, the money moves each month without you doing anything. You can stop it at any time.
example: A $150 deposit on the first of every month.

short: A setting that puts each deposit into your chosen mix for you.
detail: When it is on, new money buys your funds on the day it arrives. When it is paused, new money waits as cash until you decide. You can turn it on or off at any time.
example: With auto-invest on, a $150 deposit buys your funds on the same day.

short: A deposit your bank sent back instead of paying it.
detail: Banks do this for a few reasons, such as the account being low that day. The money never reached your investing account, so nothing you own was sold or lost.
example: You ask for a $150 deposit on the 1st, and it comes back on the 3rd.

short: Money in your account that is not invested yet.
detail: Cash does not go down when the market drops. It also does not grow when the market goes up.
example: A new deposit waits as cash until it is used to buy a stock or crypto.

short: A short code for a stock or a crypto, a bit like a username.
detail: Tickers are a few letters long. Stocks and crypto each have their own.
example: AAPL is the ticker for Apple. BTC is the ticker for Bitcoin.

short: One unit of a stock or a crypto that you can buy or sell.
detail: Each share has a price. When the price goes up, every share you own is worth more.
example: If one share costs $50 and you own 2 shares, you have $100.

short: A piece of one share, so you can invest a small amount.
detail: You do not need to buy a whole share. If a share costs $100, you can still invest $10 and own one tenth of a share.
example: $10 buys 0.1 of a $100 share. With crypto, $12 can buy a tiny part of one Bitcoin.

short: What one share costs at the latest price.
detail: Stock prices change on each day the market is open. On weekends and holidays, you see the last price from when it was open. Crypto trades every day.
example: A share might cost $95 on Monday and $97 on Friday.

short: What your shares are worth at the latest price.
detail: It is the number of shares you own times the latest price. It moves each time the price moves.
example: 3 shares at $20 each have a value of $60.

short: The total of your deposits that went through.
detail: It does not count deposits that were sent back. Compare it with your balance to see how much the market added or took away.
example: You put in $500, then $150 five times. That adds up to $1,250.

short: The total amount you spent to buy an investment.
detail: Compare it with the investment's value today. If the value is higher, you are up. If it is lower, you are down.
example: You spent $60 on a stock that is now worth $66. You are up $6.

short: How much more or less your money is worth than what you put in.
detail: Being up means it grew. Being down means it shrank. Until you sell, it can still change.
example: You put in $100 and it is worth $105. You are up $5.

short: How much your money grew or shrank, shown as a percent.
detail: A percent makes it easy to compare big and small amounts. A 5% return on $100 is $5. A 5% return on $1,000 is $50.
example: Up $5 on $100 is a 5% return.

short: A small payment some companies make to the people who own their stock.
detail: A company can share part of what it earns with its owners. It pays a set amount for each share you owned before a certain date. In First Leaf, the payment lands in your cash.
example: A company pays 27 cents a share. If you own 2 shares, you get 54 cents.

short: A small piece of a company that you can own.
detail: When the company does well, its stock can grow. It can also drop fast. That is why stocks have ups and downs.
example: Owning one share of Apple means you own a tiny piece of Apple.

short: Digital money that no government or bank runs.
detail: Crypto lives on a network of computers. Its price can swing a lot in a single day. It trades every day, even on weekends.
example: Bitcoin and Ethereum are two kinds of crypto.

short: The first and best-known crypto.
detail: Bitcoin started in 2009. No company runs it. You can own a tiny part of one Bitcoin.
example: $18 can buy a small part of one Bitcoin.

short: Help getting your stocks and cash back if your brokerage firm fails.
detail: If a brokerage firm that is a SIPC member fails, SIPC works to give back your stocks and cash, up to $500,000. That includes up to $250,000 in cash. It does not cover a drop in prices. It does not cover crypto like Bitcoin or Ethereum.
example: If your firm closed and your shares went missing, SIPC would work to get them back to you.

short: How your money is split between stocks, crypto and cash.
detail: Each part moves in its own way. Crypto usually jumps around more than stocks. Cash does not move with the market. You pick the split.
example: A mix of 80% stocks and 20% crypto.

short: Owning many different things so one bad one hurts you less.
detail: If one company has a bad year, the others can help balance it out.
example: Owning five companies instead of just one.

short: How much an investment's price tends to jump around.
detail: We rate each one from 1, calm, to 5, bumpy, using how much its price moved each day over the past year. Bumpy ones can grow more over time, but they can also fall more on a bad day.
example: Costco is a 1. Solana is a 5.

short: When your money earns money, and then that new money earns money too.
detail: It starts small and speeds up over time, like a snowball rolling downhill. The more years it has, the bigger it gets.
example: $100 that grows 6% becomes $106. The next year, the 6% is on $106, not $100.

short: The short wait after you buy or sell before the trade is final.
detail: In the U.S., most trades are final one business day later. Until then, the trade shows as settling.
example: You buy on Monday. It is final on Tuesday.

source.label: Investor.gov: New T+1 settlement cycle (U.S. SEC)

short: Whether your deposits are keeping up with your plan.
detail: It only looks at the money you put in. It does not change when the market goes up or down.
example: You planned to put in $1,400 by now and put in $1,250. You are $150 behind.

short: Practice money for trying things before you do them for real.
detail: You start with $1,000 in practice money. Nothing you do here touches your account, and you can start over at any time.
example: Buy a stock with practice money and see how it would have moved.

short: All the people buying and selling investments.
detail: When more people want to buy, prices go up. When more people want to sell, prices go down. The stock market is open on weekdays, but not on some holidays. Crypto trades every day.
example: Prices can change every minute while the market is open.
